title: Internet Group Management Protocol, Version 3
summary: Specifies IGMPv3, the protocol IPv4 systems use to tell neighboring multicast routers which multicast groups they want to join. Version 3 adds source filtering, so a host can ask for traffic only from certain senders, or from everyone except certain senders. It updates RFC 2236 and was replaced by RFC 9776.

plainLanguage.summary: When you want to watch a broadcast, you tell the nearby router you want to join. Version 3 lets you also say only from this sender, or anyone but that one.

questions: how does igmp source filtering work
how do hosts join ipv4 multicast groups
what is the difference between igmpv2 and igmpv3
what ip address do igmpv3 reports use
subtitle: How IPv4 hosts tell routers which multicast groups, and which senders, they want to hear from.

tldr.problem: Multicast routers need to know which groups the systems on each attached network want to receive, and earlier IGMP versions could not say which senders were wanted.
tldr.mechanism: Routers send periodic Queries and hosts answer with Version 3 Membership Reports that carry a group, a filter mode (INCLUDE or EXCLUDE) and a list of source addresses.
tldr.outcome: IGMPv3 adds source filtering while staying interoperable with Versions 1 and 2. The RFC was later obsoleted by RFC 9776.

today: RFC 3376 was obsoleted by RFC 9776, so that is now the place to look for the current IGMPv3 specification. According to the unit metadata it was also updated by RFC 4604, and it updates RFC 2236.

sections.title: What IGMP Does and What Version 3 Adds
sections.content:
The Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) is used by IPv4 hosts and routers to report their IP multicast group memberships to neighboring multicast routers. A router that is itself a group member performs both the router part and the group member part of the protocol.

Version 1 was specified in RFC 1112 and Version 2 in RFC 2236, which added low leave latency, a shorter time for a router to learn that a group has no members left. Version 3 adds source filtering: a system can report interest in packets only from specific source addresses, as required for Source-Specific Multicast, or from all but specific sources. The routing protocol can use this to avoid sending traffic from specific sources to networks with no interested receivers. IPv6 uses Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD) in a similar way.
sections.plainLanguage: Hosts tell nearby routers which groups they want to join. Version 3 adds the ability to pick which senders to listen to, so the router does not send you stuff you do not want.

sections.title: The Service Interface and Reception State
sections.content:
Inside a host, programs ask for multicast reception through a conceptual operation, IPMulticastListen(socket, interface, multicast-address, filter-mode, source-list). The filter-mode is INCLUDE (only the listed sources) or EXCLUDE (everyone except the listed sources). An implementation may limit source list size, but the limit MUST NOT be less than 64 addresses per list. Each new request for the same socket, interface and address completely replaces the earlier one.

The old Join and Leave operations map onto this: Join is EXCLUDE with an empty list, and Leave is INCLUDE with an empty list.

The host also derives a per-interface record from all its sockets. If every socket uses INCLUDE, the interface record is INCLUDE with the union of the source lists. If any socket uses EXCLUDE, the record is EXCLUDE with the intersection of the EXCLUDE lists minus any source that an INCLUDE socket wants. For example, INCLUDE {a, b, c} on one socket and INCLUDE {b, c, d} on another give INCLUDE {a, b, c, d} for the interface.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine two kids in a house each saying which channels they want. The house's TV box has to receive every channel that either of them asked for, and then each kid only gets their own.

sections.title: Query and Report Messages
sections.content:
IGMP messages ride in IPv4 datagrams with IP protocol number 2, an IP Time-to-Live of 1 and the IP Router Alert option. The two IGMPv3 message types are the 0x11 Membership Query and the 0x22 Version 3 Membership Report. Implementations MUST also support the Version 1 Report (0x12), the Version 2 Report (0x16) and the Version 2 Leave Group (0x17) for interoperation. Unrecognized types are silently ignored.

A Query is sent by routers. A General Query (Group Address zero, no sources) is sent to 224.0.0.1 and asks for all state; a Group-Specific Query asks about one group; a Group-and-Source-Specific Query asks whether anyone wants a group from a list of sources. The Max Resp Code field limits how long hosts may wait before answering, in tenths of a second, and values of 128 or more use a floating-point form.

A Report goes to 224.0.0.22 and holds a number of Group Records, each with a Record Type, a multicast address and a list of sources. Current-State records (types 1 and 2) answer Queries. Filter-Mode-Change records (types 3 and 4) and Source-List-Change records (types 5 and 6) announce changes. Checksums must be verified before processing.
sections.plainLanguage: The router asks 'who wants what?' and the hosts fill in a form listing the groups and the senders they care about. Another kind of form tells the router when you change your mind.

sections.title: How Members and Routers Behave
sections.content:
When a host's reception state changes, it immediately sends a State-Change Report and repeats it [Robustness Variable] - 1 more times at random intervals, in case a router missed it. When a host receives a Query it does not answer at once. It waits a random delay up to the Max Resp Time, and combines pending responses where it can, to avoid a burst of replies.

Routers keep, per group and per attached network, a filter-mode, a group timer and a list of source records with source timers. They need to know only that at least one system wants a given source, not each host's wishes. A router sends General Queries periodically and, when it learns a system is leaving or dropping a source, it sends Group-Specific or Group-and-Source-Specific Queries before it stops forwarding. One querier per subnet is elected, as in IGMPv2, and the router with the lowest IP address wins.

The information is handed to the multicast routing protocol, which makes the actual forwarding decision. Default timers include a Robustness Variable of 2, a Query Interval of 125 seconds, a Query Response Interval of 10 seconds and an Unsolicited Report Interval of 1 second.
sections.plainLanguage: When you change your mind, you tell the router a couple of times just in case it missed you. When the router asks a question, you wait a random moment to answer so everyone does not shout at once.

sections.title: Working With Older IGMP Versions
sections.content:
IGMPv3 hosts and routers interoperate with Version 1 and 2 systems. The version of a Query is told apart by size: an 8-octet message with a zero Max Resp Code is Version 1, an 8-octet message with a non-zero code is Version 2, and a message of 12 octets or more is Version 3. A Query of any other length is silently ignored.

Hosts MUST keep per-interface compatibility state and fall back to Version 1 or 2 behavior when they hear an older Query. Routers MUST implement Versions 1 and 2 too, and internally translate older messages: a Version 2 Report becomes IS_EX({}) and a Version 2 Leave becomes TO_IN({}). If a router hears an older Query it MUST use the oldest IGMP version on the network.
sections.plainLanguage: If some neighbors only speak the older language, the new devices switch to that older language so everyone can still understand each other.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC walks through the effect of a forged message of each type and describes using IPsec AH to authenticate messages if desired. A forged Query from a machine with a lower IP address than the current querier makes the forger the querier, and if it ignores Leave messages, traffic may keep flowing to groups with no members for up to the Group Membership Interval. Forged Group-and-Source-Specific Queries with large source lists and long response times could also be used for a denial of service against a host.

To defend against Queries from outside the local network, routers SHOULD NOT forward Queries, hosts SHOULD ignore Version 2 or 3 Queries without the Router Alert option, and hosts SHOULD ignore General Queries sent to a multicast address other than 224.0.0.1. A forged Report can make routers think a group has members, and the RFC suggests ignoring Reports whose source address is not on the receiving network, with 0.0.0.0 still accepted.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could pretend to be the router or a host and send fake messages. The rules say to ignore messages that come from the wrong place or lack the right marker.

fields.name: Max Resp Code
fields.desc: Maximum time before responding, in tenths of a second (floating-point form at 128 or more).

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: 16-bit one's complement checksum of the whole IGMP message.

fields.name: Group Address
fields.desc: Zero in a General Query; the queried multicast address otherwise.

fields.name: Resv
fields.desc: Set to zero on transmission, ignored on reception.

fields.name: QRV
fields.desc: Querier's Robustness Variable; zero if it exceeds 7.

fields.name: QQIC
fields.desc: Querier's Query Interval Code, in seconds.

viz.caption: GROUP RECORD TYPES IN A VERSION 3 REPORT

items.label: MODE_IS_INCLUDE
items.desc: Current state: filter mode INCLUDE with the listed sources.

items.label: MODE_IS_EXCLUDE
items.desc: Current state: filter mode EXCLUDE with the listed sources.

items.label: CHANGE_TO_INCLUDE_MODE
items.desc: The interface changed to INCLUDE mode.

items.label: CHANGE_TO_EXCLUDE_MODE
items.desc: The interface changed to EXCLUDE mode.

items.label: ALLOW_NEW_SOURCES
items.desc: Additional sources the system wants to hear from.

items.label: BLOCK_OLD_SOURCES
items.desc: Sources the system no longer wants to hear from.

messages.label: Version 3 Report to 224.0.0.22
messages.note: Sent after a random delay up to Max Resp Time; carries Current-State records.
